why_how.text: It is against the law for a driver to read or send messages while driving.
Vermont law forbids a driver from using a portable electronic device while operating a vehicle on a public highway, and the ban still applies when the vehicle is stopped.
The device ban applies even while the vehicle is stopped on a public highway, so waiting at a red light is not an exception.

A first violation of the portable electronic device law carries a fine of at least one hundred dollars and at most two hundred dollars, and a second or later violation a fine of at least two hundred fifty dollars and at most five hundred dollars.
A first handheld device violation costs one hundred to two hundred dollars, while a repeat violation costs two hundred fifty to five hundred dollars.

A conviction for using a portable electronic device while driving in a properly designated work zone with construction, maintenance or utility personnel present adds two points to the driving record for a first conviction and five points for a second or later conviction.
Points for handheld device use attach only to convictions inside a designated work zone with workers present, two for a first and five for a repeat, while the fines apply everywhere.
Driving requires full attention, so if a call must be made ask a passenger to place it or stop at a safe place first.

why_how.text: Studies show that anything that takes attention away from driving can result in a crash, and distracted drivers all show the same basic behavior of reacting more slowly to events such as a vehicle stopping to turn left or pulling out from a side road.
Distracted drivers more often fail to notice hazards such as pedestrians, bicyclists or debris, and they shrink their margin of safety, taking risks like turning left in front of oncoming traffic.
Inattention and failure to yield are the most common driver actions contributing to pedestrian and bicycle crashes in Vermont.

why_how.text: Pre program your favorite radio stations and keep the stereo low enough to hear sounds outside the vehicle such as a siren, a horn or a train whistle.
Let a front seat passenger act as co pilot instead of fumbling with maps or navigation, and when driving alone map the destination in advance.
Avoid eating and drinking while driving, keep food items secure and make sure drinks fit firmly in cup holders.
Do not underestimate how distracting children can be in the vehicle, and teach them the importance of good behavior while riding.
Take a break if you find yourself lost in thought while driving, and focus on driving rather than people or objects inside or outside the vehicle.
Do personal grooming at home rather than in the vehicle, keep pets in a carrier rather than in your lap or loose, and avoid smoking while driving because it is a distraction.

why_how.text: Emotions affect safe driving, and you may not drive well when overly worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed, so give yourself time to cool off and calm down, for example by taking a walk.
Strong emotion is handled by cooling off before driving, while running late is handled by leaving early, two different cures for two different risks.
Plan ahead and leave a few minutes early, because a driver with plenty of time is less likely to speed, break laws or crash.
